clinicalPearls: This is a syndrome, not a single disease, in which excessive loss of plasma proteins into the gastrointestinal tract leads to hypoproteinaemia and oedema.
It should be suspected in a child with hypoalbuminaemia and oedema once liver disease, kidney protein loss, and inadequate intake have been excluded.
Underlying mechanisms fall into two broad groups: lymphatic obstruction or elevated lymphatic pressure, and mucosal disease with increased permeability or erosion.

Lymphatic causes include intestinal lymphangiectasia and elevated central venous pressure after cardiac surgery (notably the Fontan circulation), while mucosal causes include inflammatory, allergic, infectious, and infiltrative enteropathies.
Because losses are non-selective, other serum proteins such as immunoglobulins and clotting factors may also fall, sometimes causing lymphopenia and predisposing to infection.
A stool alpha-1-antitrypsin measurement is a useful non-invasive marker of enteric protein loss because it is not degraded in the gut.
Management is directed at the underlying cause together with nutritional support, and in lymphatic causes a low-fat diet enriched with medium-chain triglycerides can reduce lymphatic protein loss.
Peripheral oedema, ascites, or effusions in a child with unexplained low albumin should prompt evaluation of the gut as a source.
reference.pathophysiology: Plasma proteins normally enter the gut lumen only in small amounts. In protein-losing enteropathy this loss is markedly increased by one of two general processes. In lymphatic disorders, obstructed or high-pressure intestinal lymphatics (from congenital lymphangiectasia or raised systemic venous pressure, as after Fontan surgery) leak protein-rich lymph into the lumen. In mucosal disorders, inflammation, ulceration, or increased epithelial permeability from infectious, allergic, inflammatory, or infiltrative disease allows serum proteins to escape across the damaged barrier. Because the loss is non-selective, albumin, immunoglobulins, and other proteins are depleted, producing hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, and sometimes immune compromise.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic liver disease with impaired synthesis
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis to exclude renal protein loss
Endoscopy with biopsy when mucosal disease is suspected
Imaging or echocardiography to assess lymphatics and cardiac status
redFlags: Severe hypoalbuminaemia with anasarca, ascites, or effusions
Signs of immunodeficiency or recurrent infection from immunoglobulin loss
Evidence of underlying serious cardiac or lymphatic disease
Features of an underlying inflammatory or malignant infiltrative process
reference.prognosis: Outlook depends heavily on the underlying cause; some mucosal causes resolve when the primary disease is treated, whereas lymphangiectasia and Fontan-associated protein loss can be chronic and difficult to manage.
pitfalls: Attributing hypoalbuminaemia and oedema to renal or hepatic causes without considering the gut
Overlooking accompanying immunoglobulin loss and infection risk
Failing to identify and treat the specific underlying disorder
Neglecting nutritional support and the role of a low-fat, medium-chain triglyceride diet in lymphatic loss
management: Direct treatment at the underlying cause, for example immunosuppression for inflammatory bowel disease or an elimination diet for allergic enteropathy
For intestinal lymphangiectasia, institute a low-fat diet enriched with medium-chain triglycerides to reduce lymphatic protein loss, with dietitian support
In Fontan-associated protein-losing enteropathy, optimise the circulation and consider therapies such as heparin, budesonide, pulmonary vasodilators or Fontan revision
Provide nutritional support with adequate protein and energy, and use intravenous albumin and immunoglobulin replacement when clinically indicated
Monitor for infection resulting from immunoglobulin and lymphocyte loss, and manage oedema with attention to fluid balance
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across paediatric gastroenterology, cardiology, dietetics and immunology
